stem: What does Newton's Third Law state?

choices.label: A
choices.text: For every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force
choices.explanation: Newton's Third Law: forces come in action-reaction pairs of equal magnitude and opposite direction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An object in motion stays in motion unless acted on by a net force
choices.explanation: This describes Newton's FIRST Law (inertia), not the Third Law.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Force equals mass times acceleration
choices.explanation: This describes Newton's SECOND Law (F=ma), not the Third Law.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Objects with greater mass always exert greater forces
choices.explanation: This isn't a correct statement of any of Newton's laws -- the Third Law is about action-reaction pairs, regardless of mass.

explanation: Newton's Third Law states that for every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force.

stem: Action-reaction force pairs (Newton's Third Law) act on which object(s)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Two different objects -- the action force acts on one object, the reaction force acts on the other
choices.explanation: Action-reaction pairs always act on two DIFFERENT objects, which is why they never cancel each other out for a single object's motion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both forces act on the same object
choices.explanation: This is a common misconception -- if both forces acted on the same object, they would always cancel out, making acceleration impossible.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither force acts on any physical object
choices.explanation: Both the action and reaction forces are real forces acting on real, physical objects.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only the heavier of the two objects experiences a force
choices.explanation: Both objects experience a force of EQUAL magnitude, regardless of their relative masses.

explanation: Action-reaction pairs act on two different objects, which is why they don't cancel out within a single object's free-body diagram.

stem: A person pushes against a wall with a force of 50 N. What is the reaction force, according to Newton's Third Law?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The wall pushes back on the person with 50 N in the opposite direction
choices.explanation: The reaction force is equal in magnitude (50 N) and opposite in direction, exerted by the wall on the person.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The wall pushes back on the person with 25 N
choices.explanation: The reaction force must be EQUAL in magnitude to the action force (50 N), not half of it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The person's own muscles create the reaction force
choices.explanation: The reaction force is exerted by the WALL on the person, not generated internally by the person's own body.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There is no reaction force since the wall doesn't move
choices.explanation: A reaction force exists regardless of whether the wall visibly moves -- the wall doesn't need to move for the force to be real.

explanation: By Newton's Third Law, the wall exerts an equal (50 N) and opposite force back on the person.

stem: When analyzing a "system" of multiple objects together (e.g., two boxes connected by a string), what happens to the internal forces between the objects in the system?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Internal forces (like the tension pulling the two boxes toward each other) cancel out when considering the system as a whole, by Newton's Third Law
choices.explanation: Internal action-reaction pairs between objects in the same system cancel out, since they act with equal magnitude in opposite directions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Internal forces always add up to twice their individual value
choices.explanation: Internal forces cancel due to being equal and opposite (Third Law pairs), not double in magnitude.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Internal forces are irrelevant and were never present
choices.explanation: Internal forces are real and important for analyzing the individual objects -- they just cancel out for the system's overall (external) net force.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Internal forces only affect the more massive object in the system
choices.explanation: Internal forces affect both objects equally in magnitude (though possibly differently in resulting acceleration, due to differing masses).

explanation: Internal forces between objects in the same system are Newton's Third Law pairs and cancel out when analyzing the system as a whole.

stem: How does a person walking forward rely on Newton's Third Law?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The person's foot pushes backward on the ground, and the ground pushes forward on the person's foot with an equal and opposite force, propelling them forward
choices.explanation: The forward reaction force from the ground (in response to the person's backward push) is what propels the person forward.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The person's muscles alone create forward motion with no external force needed
choices.explanation: Without an external reaction force from the ground (e.g., on ice with no friction), muscle contraction alone cannot produce forward motion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gravity pulls the person forward
choices.explanation: Gravity acts downward (vertically), not in the horizontal direction the person is walking.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Newton's Third Law has no relevance to walking
choices.explanation: Walking is actually a classic, direct application of Newton's Third Law via the ground-reaction force.

explanation: Walking relies on the ground's reaction force: pushing backward on the ground results in the ground pushing forward on the person.

stem: What does a free-body diagram (FBD) show?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All the forces acting ON a single object, represented as vectors from that object's center
choices.explanation: An FBD isolates one object and shows every force acting ON it (not forces it exerts on other things).

choices.label: B
choices.text: All the forces the object exerts on other objects
choices.explanation: An FBD shows forces acting ON the object, not forces the object exerts outward on other things.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The object's velocity and acceleration vectors only
choices.explanation: An FBD specifically shows FORCES, not velocity or acceleration vectors directly (though acceleration can be inferred from the net force).

choices.label: D
choices.text: A diagram of the object's internal structure
choices.explanation: An FBD is about external forces acting on the object as a whole, not its internal structure.

explanation: A free-body diagram shows all forces acting ON a single isolated object.

stem: The free-body diagram below shows a book resting motionless on a table. Why are the Normal force and Weight equal in magnitude?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The book is in equilibrium (not accelerating), so by Newton's Second Law the net force -- and thus the sum of these two vertical forces -- must be zero
choices.explanation: Since the book isn't accelerating, the net force must be zero, requiring the upward Normal force to exactly balance the downward Weight.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Normal force and Weight are always equal for any object, regardless of its motion
choices.explanation: This is only true when the object is in vertical equilibrium (not accelerating vertically) -- e.g., in an accelerating elevator, they would NOT be equal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The table pushes exactly as hard as the book weighs by definition, unrelated to Newton's laws
choices.explanation: This isn't just an arbitrary definition -- it's a direct consequence of Newton's Second Law applied to a non-accelerating object.

choices.label: D
choices.text: This is a coincidence specific to books
choices.explanation: This isn't a coincidence or specific to books -- it follows generally from Newton's Second Law for any object in vertical equilibrium.

explanation: Since the book isn't accelerating, Newton's Second Law requires the net force to be zero, so the Normal force must equal the Weight.

diagram.altText: Free-body diagram of a book with the Normal force pointing up and Weight pointing down, equal in length

stem: The free-body diagram below shows a box being pulled to the right by an applied force, with friction opposing the motion. Based on the relative lengths of the vectors shown, what is the direction of the net force on the box?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To the right, since the applied force is larger than the friction force
choices.explanation: The applied force vector is drawn longer than the friction vector, so the net horizontal force points in the direction of the larger (applied) force -- to the right.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To the left, since friction always dominates
choices.explanation: Friction does not always dominate; here the applied force vector is clearly drawn longer, indicating it's the larger force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There is no net force -- the box is in equilibrium
choices.explanation: The two horizontal vectors are drawn with different lengths (unequal magnitudes), so they don't cancel -- there IS a net force.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The net force direction cannot be determined from a free-body diagram
choices.explanation: A free-body diagram's vector lengths are specifically meant to convey relative force magnitudes, which do let you determine net force direction.

explanation: Since the applied force vector is longer (larger) than the friction vector, the net force points to the right, in the applied force's direction.

diagram.altText: Free-body diagram of a box with a larger applied force pointing right and a smaller friction force pointing left

stem: Which of the following would NOT correctly appear on the free-body diagram of a box resting on the floor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The force the box exerts on the floor
choices.explanation: This force acts ON the floor, not on the box -- it belongs on the floor's own FBD (or is simply the Third Law reaction pair to the Normal force on the box), not the box's.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The weight of the box (gravity pulling down on it)
choices.explanation: Weight is a force acting ON the box, and correctly belongs on its free-body diagram.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The normal force from the floor pushing up on the box
choices.explanation: The normal force acts ON the box (from the floor), and correctly belongs on its free-body diagram.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Friction from the floor acting on the box, if the box is being pushed
choices.explanation: Friction from the floor acts ON the box, and correctly belongs on its free-body diagram if applicable.

explanation: An FBD shows forces acting ON the object -- the force the box exerts on the floor acts on the floor, not on the box, so it doesn't belong.

stem: An object falls through the air, and air resistance is negligible. What does the free-body diagram of the object look like during the fall?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single downward vector representing the object's weight -- no other forces act on it
choices.explanation: With air resistance neglected, gravity (weight) is the only force acting on the falling object.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two vectors: weight downward and a supporting normal force upward
choices.explanation: There is no surface in contact with the object while it's falling through the air, so there's no normal force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two equal and opposite vectors that cancel out completely
choices.explanation: If forces canceled out completely, the object wouldn't accelerate -- but a freely falling object DOES accelerate due to unbalanced weight.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No vectors at all, since the object is in the air
choices.explanation: Being in the air doesn't mean no forces act -- gravity (weight) still acts on the object throughout the fall.

explanation: With air resistance neglected, weight is the only force acting on a freely falling object.

stem: In a free-body diagram, the normal force between two surfaces in contact always points in which direction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Perpendicular to (directly away from) the contact surface
choices.explanation: The normal force is, by definition, always perpendicular to the surface of contact.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Always straight up, regardless of the surface's orientation
choices.explanation: The normal force is perpendicular to the SURFACE, not always straight up -- on an incline, for example, it points away from the tilted surface, not vertically.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Always parallel to the contact surface
choices.explanation: This describes the direction of FRICTION, not the normal force, which is specifically perpendicular to the surface.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the same direction as the object's velocity
choices.explanation: The normal force's direction is determined by the surface's orientation, not by the object's velocity direction.

explanation: The normal force is always perpendicular to the surface of contact.

stem: The free-body diagram below shows a block on a frictionless incline, with the Normal force perpendicular to the incline surface and Weight straight down. Which force (or component of a force) is responsible for the block accelerating down the incline?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The component of the Weight that points along the incline surface (parallel to it)
choices.explanation: The Normal force is entirely perpendicular to the incline and has no component along it; only Weight has a component along the incline's surface, which causes the block to accelerate down the slope.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The full Normal force vector
choices.explanation: The Normal force is entirely perpendicular to the incline surface and has zero component along it, so it cannot cause acceleration down the slope.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The full Weight vector, exactly as drawn (straight down)
choices.explanation: Only the COMPONENT of Weight along the incline surface matters for motion along the incline -- not the full straight-down vector.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither force has any component along the incline
choices.explanation: Weight does have a nonzero component along the incline (unless the incline is perfectly flat), which is exactly what accelerates the block.

explanation: Only the component of Weight parallel to the incline surface contributes to acceleration along the incline; the Normal force is entirely perpendicular to it.

diagram.altText: Free-body diagram of a block on an incline with the Normal force perpendicular to the incline surface and Weight pointing straight down

stem: What does Newton's First Law (the law of inertia) state?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion at constant velocity, unless acted upon by a net external force
choices.explanation: This is the standard statement of Newton's First Law -- the law of inertia.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Force equals mass times acceleration
choices.explanation: This describes Newton's SECOND Law, not the First Law.

choices.label: C
choices.text: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction
choices.explanation: This describes Newton's THIRD Law, not the First Law.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Objects always eventually come to rest due to their own inertia
choices.explanation: This misrepresents inertia -- inertia is the tendency to RESIST changes in motion, not a tendency to naturally slow down.

explanation: Newton's First Law: an object's velocity stays constant unless acted upon by a net external force.

stem: An object moves at a constant velocity of 5 m/s in a straight line. What must be true about the net force acting on it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The net force must be zero
choices.explanation: By Newton's First Law, constant velocity (zero acceleration) means the net force must be zero.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The net force must equal the object's mass times 5
choices.explanation: This would only apply if the object were accelerating at 5 m/s²; constant velocity means zero acceleration, and thus zero net force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The net force must be in the direction of motion
choices.explanation: If a nonzero net force existed in the direction of motion, the object would be SPEEDING UP, not moving at constant velocity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The net force cannot be determined without knowing the object's mass
choices.explanation: Regardless of mass, constant velocity always implies zero net force -- no additional information is needed.

explanation: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, which by Newton's First/Second Law means the net force is zero.

stem: An object is in equilibrium (net force = 0) under the action of three forces. Two of the forces are 8 N to the right and 3 N to the left. What must the third force be?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 5 N to the left
choices.explanation: For equilibrium, all forces must sum to zero: 8 N right - 3 N left = 5 N net right, so the third force must be 5 N to the left to cancel it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 5 N to the right
choices.explanation: This would make the net force 10 N to the right, not zero -- the third force must oppose the existing net force, not add to it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 11 N to the left
choices.explanation: This incorrectly adds the two given force magnitudes rather than finding their net effect first.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 0 N (no third force needed)
choices.explanation: Without a third force, the net of the given two forces (8N right, 3N left) is 5N right, not zero -- so a third force IS needed for equilibrium.

explanation: The existing two forces sum to 5 N net to the right; the third force must be 5 N to the left to bring the net to zero.

stem: What is "inertia"?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An object's tendency to resist a change in its state of motion, proportional to its mass
choices.explanation: Inertia is the resistance to changes in motion, and it scales directly with an object's mass.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A type of force that pushes objects forward
choices.explanation: Inertia isn't a force at all -- it's a property (resistance to changes in motion) that objects possess due to their mass.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The speed at which an object naturally moves
choices.explanation: Inertia doesn't describe or determine a natural speed -- it describes resistance to changes in motion, regardless of what that motion currently is.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A force that only applies to moving objects, not stationary ones
choices.explanation: Inertia applies to ALL objects, whether at rest or in motion -- both resist changes to their current state.

explanation: Inertia is an object's tendency to resist changes in its motion, proportional to its mass.

stem: A hockey puck slides across frictionless ice at constant velocity. According to Newton's First Law, what force is required to keep it moving?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No additional force is required -- the puck continues at constant velocity on its own due to inertia
choices.explanation: With no net force (frictionless surface), the puck's inertia keeps it moving at constant velocity indefinitely, with no force needed to sustain the motion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A continuously applied force in the direction of motion is required
choices.explanation: This is a common misconception -- constant velocity requires ZERO net force, not a continuously applied force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A force equal to the puck's weight is required
choices.explanation: The puck's weight is already balanced by the normal force from the ice; no additional horizontal force is needed to sustain constant velocity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The puck will naturally slow down and stop even without friction
choices.explanation: Without friction (or any other force), the puck will NOT naturally slow down -- it continues at constant velocity by inertia.

explanation: No force is needed to sustain constant velocity motion; inertia keeps the puck moving in the absence of a net force.

stem: A 5 kg object accelerates at $4 \text{ m/s}^2$. What net force is acting on it?

choices.label: B
choices.text: 9 N
choices.explanation: This adds the mass and acceleration values rather than multiplying them.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This incorrectly divides mass by acceleration rather than multiplying them.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This incorrectly divides acceleration by mass rather than multiplying mass by acceleration.

explanation: Using F = ma: F = (5)(4) = 20 N.

stem: A net force of 18 N acts on a 3 kg object. What is its acceleration?

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This incorrectly multiplies F and m rather than dividing F by m.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This incorrectly subtracts m from F rather than dividing.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This incorrectly divides m by F rather than F by m.

explanation: Using a = F/m: a = 18/3 = 6 m/s².

stem: A net force of 24 N gives an object an acceleration of $6 \text{ m/s}^2$. What is the object's mass?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 4 kg

choices.label: B
choices.text: 144 kg
choices.explanation: This incorrectly multiplies F and a rather than dividing F by a.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 18 kg
choices.explanation: This incorrectly subtracts a from F rather than dividing.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This incorrectly divides a by F rather than F by a.

explanation: Using m = F/a: m = 24/6 = 4 kg.

stem: A 4 kg object experiences two horizontal forces: 30 N to the right and 10 N to the left. What is the object's acceleration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 5 m/s^2 to the right
choices.explanation: Net force = 30 - 10 = 20 N to the right. a = F_net/m = 20/4 = 5 m/s² to the right.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 10 m/s^2 to the right
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly divide the net force (20N) by the mass (4kg).

choices.label: C
choices.text: 7.5 m/s^2 to the right
choices.explanation: This incorrectly adds the two forces (40N) instead of finding their net difference (20N) before dividing by mass.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 2.5 m/s^2 to the left
choices.explanation: This has both the magnitude and direction wrong -- the larger force (30N) is to the right, so the net force and acceleration are to the right, not left.

explanation: Net force = 30-10 = 20 N right; a = F_net/m = 20/4 = 5 m/s² to the right.

stem: The same net force is applied to two different objects: Object A has twice the mass of Object B. How do their accelerations compare?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Object A's acceleration is half of Object B's acceleration
choices.explanation: Since a=F/m and F is the same for both, acceleration is inversely proportional to mass -- doubling the mass halves the acceleration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Object A's acceleration is double Object B's acceleration
choices.explanation: This reverses the correct inverse relationship between mass and acceleration for a fixed force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Their accelerations are equal
choices.explanation: Since acceleration depends on mass (a=F/m) and their masses differ, their accelerations cannot be equal under the same force.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There's no relationship between mass and acceleration for a fixed force
choices.explanation: There IS a clear, direct inverse relationship: a=F/m, so mass and acceleration are inversely proportional for a fixed force.

explanation: Since a=F/m, doubling the mass (with the same force) halves the acceleration.

stem: What is the weight of a 10 kg object ($g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$)?

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is just the mass value; weight must be computed as mass times g.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This adds mass and g rather than multiplying them.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This incorrectly divides mass by g rather than multiplying.

stem: A block slides down a frictionless incline angled at 30° above horizontal ($g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2$). What is the block's acceleration along the incline?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: On a frictionless incline, a = g·sin(θ) = 9.8·sin(30°) = 9.8(0.5) = 4.9 m/s².

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the full value of g, without multiplying by sin(30°) to project it along the incline.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This uses cos(30°) instead of sin(30°) -- the component ALONG the incline uses sine of the incline angle, not cosine.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 4.9 m/s^2, but directed horizontally
choices.explanation: While the magnitude is correct, the acceleration is directed ALONG the incline surface, not purely horizontally.

explanation: On a frictionless incline, a = g·sin(θ) = 9.8·sin(30°) ≈ 4.9 m/s², directed along the incline.

stem: Two masses, $m_1 = 5$ kg and $m_2 = 3$ kg, are connected by a string over a frictionless, massless pulley (an Atwood machine, $g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2$). What is the magnitude of the system's acceleration?

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is just g itself, ignoring the fact that both masses partially counterbalance each other in an Atwood machine.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is half the correct value -- likely from an error in the (m1+m2) denominator.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly apply the Atwood machine formula using both masses in the numerator and denominator.

explanation: For an Atwood machine, a = (m1-m2)g/(m1+m2) = (2)(9.8)/8 = 2.45 m/s².

stem: A box on a surface has a normal force of 50 N and a coefficient of friction of 0.3. What is the magnitude of the friction force?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Friction = μN = (0.3)(50) = 15 N.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This adds μ and N rather than multiplying them.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This incorrectly divides N by μ rather than multiplying μ by N.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This incorrectly divides μ by N rather than multiplying them.

explanation: Friction = μN = (0.3)(50) = 15 N.

stem: A 5 kg box is pulled horizontally by an applied force of 20 N, while friction of 5 N opposes the motion. What is the box's acceleration?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Net force = 20-5 = 15 N. a = F_net/m = 15/5 = 3 m/s².

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This ignores the friction force entirely, using only the applied force divided by mass.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly compute the net force (20-5=15N) before dividing by mass.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly apply F_net=ma using the given applied force, friction, and mass.

explanation: Net force = 20-5 = 15 N; a = 15/5 = 3 m/s².

stem: Two boxes, $m_1=2$ kg and $m_2=3$ kg, are connected by a string and sit on a frictionless surface. A horizontal force of 15 N pulls $m_2$, which pulls $m_1$ via the connecting string. What is the tension in the string connecting the two boxes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 6 N
choices.explanation: First find the system's acceleration: a = F/(m1+m2) = 15/5 = 3 m/s². The string only needs to accelerate m1: T = m1·a = (2)(3) = 6 N.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the total applied force, not the tension in the connecting string, which only needs to accelerate m1 (not the whole system).

choices.label: C
choices.text: 9 N
choices.explanation: This incorrectly uses m2 (3kg) rather than m1 (2kg) when computing T=m·a.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 3 N
choices.explanation: This is just the system's acceleration value, not multiplied by m1 to find the tension force.

explanation: System acceleration = F/(m1+m2) = 15/5 = 3 m/s². Tension = m1·a = 2(3) = 6 N.

stem: A 70 kg person stands on a scale inside an elevator accelerating upward at $2 \text{ m/s}^2$ ($g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2$). What does the scale read (the normal force on the person)?

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is just the person's normal weight (mg), ignoring the upward acceleration of the elevator.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is just ma (the extra force from acceleration), without adding the person's actual weight mg.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This incorrectly subtracts rather than adds the acceleration term -- an UPWARD accelerating elevator increases the scale reading, not decreases it.

explanation: For an upward-accelerating elevator: N = m(g+a) = 70(9.8+2) = 826 N.

stem: A block slides down an incline angled at 37° ($\sin 37°\approx 0.6$, $\cos 37°\approx 0.8$) with a coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu=0.2$ ($g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2$). What is the block's acceleration down the incline?

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is g·sinθ alone (4.9... adjusted), omitting the friction term that reduces the acceleration.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly combine the gravity and friction components along the incline.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is the full value of g, ignoring both the incline angle and friction entirely.
